title: Psalm 58:1–11
context: To the choirmaster: according to Do Not Destroy. A Miktam of David. Imprecatory challenge to unjust gods/rulers who devise wrongs and deal violence; wicked estranged from the womb, serpent venom, deaf to charm; prayer that God break teeth, dissolve snares, sweep away; the righteous rejoice at vengeance; mankind confesses reward for the righteous and a God who judges the earth. Treat both camps’ hearing as serious—not ironic.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Arminian and Reformed writers of the past on unjust judges, venomous obstinacy, imprecation that breaks the predator’s teeth, and joy at God’s vengeance that proves he judges on earth, in their own words.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: O congregation—Saul’s judges and counsellors consulting against David. Sons of men—to mind them they are men and must give account for hard speeches. Heart—with free choice and consent; Hands—great wrong under pretence of justice, weighing then turning the scale. Estranged—from God and all goodness; natures corrupt from birth; Astray—by actual sins from childhood. Poison—malicious disposition. Not hearken—deaf to counsels, conscience, and God’s law. Teeth—powerful instruments of mischief. Melt away—as snow-waters that run then are gone. Melteth—quickly dissolved. Before pots feel thorns—violently take them away, living, as Korah. Rejoice—for blessed effects: vindication of God’s honour and deliverance of good men.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Ps 58)

reformed.quote: David challenges the congregation—Saul’s counsellors—with conscious rectitude. In heart they plot wickedness; hands weigh out violence openly upon the earth. They are monsters of iniquity, wicked from the womb beyond common corruption. Their poison is like the serpent’s; deaf adders shutting ear against the charmer. Then he assumes imprecation: Break their teeth—God’s peculiar prerogative to repel oppression. Let them flow away like waters; arrows as broken; vanish like a snail; like an untimely birth. Before pots feel thorns, a whirlwind carries them away. The righteous rejoice at vengeance under holy zeal, not cruel hatred—sympathy with God’s justness. Man shall say: verily reward for the righteous; verily a God that judgeth in the earth.

verses.text: Do you indeed speak righteousness, silent ones? Do you judge blamelessly, you sons of men?
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: O congregation—Saul’s judges and counsellors; Sons of men—they must give account for hard speeches. The challenge exposes sham justice.

Rulers who claim to decree right are still accountable men. Shared seriousness—the question is not sarcasm for sport but an arraignment before God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: challenge from conscious rectitude; congregation as Saul’s assembly ostensibly for the nation, for oppression; sons of men may strip the courtesy title. Integrity may challenge kings and counsellors.

Unjust gods are weighed. Appeal to adversaries’ own lips and to God’s tribunal when the world will not hear.

verses.text: No, in your heart you plot injustice. You measure out the violence of your hands on the earth.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Heart—free choice and consent; Hands—wrong under pretence of justice, weighing then turning the scale; in this land under God and law.

Devising wrongs is willed, not fate alone. Violence “dealt out” as if measured justice is hypocrisy grace still names and resists by prayer.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: wickedness first in thoughts then practiced with hands; weigh/frame violence; upon the earth—unbridled license done openly.

Their hearts plot what their hands carry out. Pretended equity glossing oppression is still violence God sees.

verses.text: The wicked go astray from the womb. They are wayward as soon as they are born, speaking lies.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Estranged—from God and goodness; natures corrupt from birth, wicked offspring of sinful parents; Astray—actual sins from childhood when reason begins.

Original corruption and early actual sin both named. Estrangement deepens by lies spoken; the will goes astray as capacity grows—serious diagnosis, not excuse for cruelty.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: not recent sinners but born to commit sin; leavened with wickedness from the womb. All inherit Adam’s stain, yet some proceed to intolerable iniquity—monsters beyond common restraint.

From-the-womb language is grave anthropology. Both camps refuse to soft-pedal congenital and early deceit.
verses.keyContrast: Both take estrangement from the womb with full seriousness. Arminians stress free consent and actual sins stacking on corrupt nature; Reformed readers stress radical native wickedness and a class of intolerable iniquity under Adam’s stain.

verses.text: Their poison is like the poison of a snake, like a deaf cobra that stops its ear,
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Poison—malicious disposition. Serpent and deaf adder picture willful malice that will not hear.

Venom is moral, not merely “strong personality.” Stopping the ear is refusal of counsel—serious enough to drive the imprecations that follow.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: deadly malice like serpent poison; deaf adders famed for cunning against the charmer. Consummate subtlety that will not be won by wise appeal.

Serpent venom is not comic hyperbole. Both camps hear spiritual danger in deaf malice.

verses.text: which doesn’t listen to the voice of charmers, no matter how skillful the charmer may be.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Not hearken—deaf to counsels, conscience, and God’s law; adder called deaf because it will not be charmed.

Refusal to hear is culpable. Wise charming fails where the will stops the ear; prayer then turns from persuasion of the wicked to appeal to God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: enchantment figure underscores craft that resists every artifice; obstinacy against word and Spirit’s enlightenment. Persuasion exhausted, imprecation remains.

Deafness to charm is judicial seriousness.

verses.text: Break their teeth, God, in their mouth. Break out the great teeth of the young lions, LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Teeth—powerful instruments of doing mischief. Imprecation asks God to disable the predator, not private revenge.

Break teeth is serious petition for public check. Shared—both camps refuse to baptize this as mere venting; it is prayer that God disarm violence so harm stops.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: language of imprecation; vengeance is God’s peculiar prerogative after integrity asserted. Teeth and lion jaws—wild-beast desire to rend; crush and restrain rage.

Imprecation is prayer to the Judge. God alone breaks fangs; the saint does not take the lion’s mouth in hand.
verses.keyContrast: Both treat break the teeth as a grave plea for God’s justice. Arminians stress that disabling the predator may yet leave room for check and turn; Reformed readers stress that God himself crushes the violence according to his righteous will.

verses.text: Let them vanish like water that flows away. When they draw the bow, let their arrows be made blunt.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Melt away—snow-waters that run with force then are suddenly gone; arrows as cut in pieces. Swift nullifying of threat.

Vanishing and blunting are asked so malice fails mid-aim. Serious hope—God may evaporate the flood and snap the shaft before it strikes.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: flow away like waters—swiftly; faith that solid national opposition melt before God. Arrows fall powerless as broken though the bow is bent.

Do not cease to pray after arrows are fitted. Both camps hear judicial seriousness: the threat is serious, and so is the plea that it dissolve.

verses.text: Let them be like a snail which melts and passes away, like the stillborn child, who has not seen the sun.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Melteth—quickly dissolved; untimely birth that may not see the sun. Evaporation of proud schemes.

Snail and stillborn images are severe—not to be softened into comedy. Shared seriousness—malice’s career may be cut off before it “has not seen the sun” of success.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: snail melting; abortion—pass away before life well begun; God can crush the mighty in a moment. Pride in easy prosperity dashed by equally sudden end.

These similes are judicial, not cruel entertainment. Both camps refuse to laugh off the stillborn image; it is prayer that evil not mature.

verses.text: Before your pots can feel the heat of the thorns, he will sweep away the green and the burning alike.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Before pots heated—take them violently and irresistibly; Living—alive, as Korah. Whirlwind judgment before schemes cook.

Sweep-away is sudden divine act. Shared—thorn-fire under pots meets storm; neither camp treats Korah-like removal as light rhetoric.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: swift judgment—before thorns grow to bush or flesh feels the pot’s heat; whirlwind carries them raw. Unprepared wickedness snatched mid-plan.

Timing of wrath outruns the cook-fire. Serious petition that God not let violence “come to a boil.”

verses.text: The righteous shall rejoice when he sees the vengeance. He shall wash his feet in the blood of the wicked,
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Rejoice—for blessed effects: vindication of God’s honour and deliverance of himself and all good men. Joy at justice’s fruit, not bloodlust.

Bathing feet in blood is martial image of complete victory under God. Shared seriousness—rejoicing is at vengeance as God’s, for honour and rescue; both camps reject sadistic glee while affirming judicial joy.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: joy under holy zeal guided by the Spirit—sympathy with God’s justness, not hatred’s desire for revenge. When obstinacy brings retribution, saints rejoice that God awards punishment and cares for their safety.

Pure joy at judgment differs from cruel satisfaction. Both camps take the verse as grave doxology over God’s vengeance, not a joke.
verses.keyContrast: Both take rejoicing at vengeance with full moral seriousness. Arminians emphasize joy for honour vindicated and good men delivered, still hoping the wicked might have turned; Reformed readers typically stress Spirit-guided delight in God’s executed justice when obstinacy has closed the door to repentance.

verses.text: so that men shall say, “Most certainly there is a reward for the righteous. Most certainly there is a God who judges the earth.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley’s arc closes in public confession: reward for the righteous; God judging on earth. The imprecations aim at this acknowledgement.

Mankind’s saying invites the watching world to learn righteousness. Shared—final verdict is theodicy spoken aloud; prayer for judgment serves confession that God still judges here.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: man shall say—saints especially, many whose faith staggered now established. Verily reward; verily God judges in the earth—against the thought that providence is only heavenly. Judgments teach righteousness (Isa 26:9).

Earthly judgment confessed. Both camps end convinced: the righteous are not abandoned; God judges on earth.
verses.keyContrast: Both end with mankind confessing reward and a judging God. Arminians stress the public invitation to learn and keep seeking righteousness; Reformed readers press that manifested judgments establish faith that providence rules the earth, not chance.
